subject: wizardBookshelf
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: wizard's bookshelf with tomes, scrolls, orbs and candles.
Style: high-fantasy anime.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a wizard's bookshelf prop with tomes, scrolls, orbs, and candles in a high-fantasy anime style, structuring it around a root joint and building parts with basic geometries, extrusions, and lathes using the SDK.

I'm sketching out the bookshelf's overall dimensions and structure — a dark wooden frame roughly 1.5m wide, 0.42m deep, and 2.1-2.35m tall with an arched crown, side posts, shelves, and back panel, then planning the decorative details: leaning books with gold bands and gem clasps, stacked scrolls, glowing orbs on lathe stands, and lathe-built candles with wax drips and flames, plus wizardy accents like a crescent moon finial and a hanging ornament. I'm now working out exact shelf heights and board positions along the vertical axis.

I'm figuring out side panel and back panel placement relative to the inner cavity width, and thinking through how to apply wood grain textures using paint helpers for a believable timber look, while keeping color usage within reasonable limits across all the books and decorative elements.

For the anime aesthetic I'm leaning into saturated purples, teals, and crimsons with gold trim, plus glowing cyan/magenta/amber orbs using a glow kit. I'm also sketching out a reusable book-generator function that builds each book from a colored cover box with inset cream pages for the spine.

Working out the cover and page geometry so the pages peek out correctly depending on which side the spine faces...

I should budget around 1000 parts total, so spine decorations like gold bands and title plates need to stay modest—maybe 7 decorative parts per book across 35-40 books, roughly 280 parts, which keeps the total manageable. I'll write a helper box function that creates part geometry with color and bone attachment to the root joint, simplifying repeated calls.

For tilted books, I need to handle rotation manually: each subpart's local offset gets rotated around the book's base pivot using standard 2D rotation math, then the part itself gets a z-axis rotation to match the tilt angle, so the whole book leans convincingly rather than needing a separate group transform.

Since a leaning book pivots at its bottom corner rather than center, I'll compute a small vertical lift of roughly half-width times sine of the tilt angle to keep the bottom corner resting on the shelf surface.

Now for horizontally stacked books lying flat, I need a generic builder that handles both orientations -- upright books use thickness along x and height along y, while flat books swap those dimensions so the spine still faces outward correctly.

Working out local-to-world coordinate mapping for flat versus upright orientation, defining the pivot at bottom-center and swapping thickness/length axes accordingly, then placing the spine plate facing forward along the depth axis.

Now I'm sizing the covers and page block relative to the spine depth, recessing the pages slightly between the boards so there's a visible gap at the open end, while thinking through whether the pages should protrude slightly for a more realistic look.

I'm adding spine decoration — thin gold bands near the top and bottom of the spine, a small title plate partway down in a contrasting color, and planning a clasp for some of the larger tomes while keeping thinner ones plain.

Now I'm laying out the shelf compartments: setting board positions and thicknesses (B0 through B4, with the top one doubling as the roof), then computing the open height of each compartment between boards — roughly 0.48, 0.44, 0.40, and 0.36 units as they go up, since books get shorter higher up. Above the roof I'm leaving room for cornice detailing and some decorative objects like candles, an orb, or a skull.

I'm figuring out the overall proportions — about 2.4m tall with a crown arch and moon finial on a 1.5m wide shelf, which feels right for a tall wizard's bookshelf. Then I'm working out the depth placement for items inside each compartment: defining the inner x-range, the back panel position, and where book spines should sit relative to the shelf's front edge so covers look flush and natural, factoring in book depth of about 0.28 units centered near the front.

Now I'm populating the bottom compartment: a row of upright tomes on the left, a stack of flat tomes topped with a candle in the center, and an urn with scrolls jutting out tilted on the right. For the next compartment up, I'm placing a glowing cyan orb on a stand at the left side alongside some books, working out combined heights to keep everything within the shelf's bounds.

Adding the wax seal ribbon band and setting up a reusable scroll-building helper, then placing book stacks along the third shelf.

For the fourth shelf I'm arranging a cluster of varied-height stub candles on a plate near the center, more books on the left, and a large orb with an ornate gold torus ring on the right, while deciding against a lectern-style open book for being too complex.

For the top crown, I'm settling on a stack of three big tomes with a candle on top on the left, a glowing crescent moon with a star at center, and a large purple-pink orb on a stand with scrolls in a jar on the right, topped by an arch cornice. For the frame itself, I'm planning side panels with darker inset recesses and gold trim, plus corner posts with carved finials.

Now I'm detailing the finials as lathe-turned pinnacles with small orbs, a stepped-moulding cornice with a gold trim line, and bun feet on the base plinth. For decoration, I want gold trim strips along the shelf edges and glowing cyan rune textures on the side panels and pillar front faces to give it that anime magic-shop feel, positioning thin rune-textured planes on the pillar fronts.

Writing the rune SVG texture...

I'm also considering small floating gold star sparkles hovering near the orbs for an extra anime touch, making sure nothing actually hangs below the model's lowest contact point with the floor.

Writing star extrusion geometry...

Still computing the arc geometry...

Since both arcs converge at the same intersection points, I'll skip the first and last points of the inner arc to avoid duplicate coordinates, keeping the outer endpoints sharp. The crescent should open toward +x in model space, so I'm orienting the moon shape to face +Z on the crown with that axis convention.

For the candle, I'm building a lathe profile from the axis outward and back up, closing the loop with points along the base, side, and dished top, making sure x never goes negative. I'll add drip details using scaled sphere geometry stretched vertically near the top edge.

For the flame, I'm lathing a teardrop profile with an orange outer layer and a smaller inner yellow flame for glow, plus a tiny dark cylinder for the wick. For the candle holder, I'm deciding between flat gold colors versus metal paint for brass trims, leaning toward flat colors on small parts since metal paint tends to blur fine detail, while using metal paint for larger brass elements.

For the big frame pieces, I'm checking paint-sheet resolution across the large surface area and confirming 1024 texels is sufficient without needing 2048. I'm planning wood grain textures—horizontal grain for shelves, vertical for sides—using a deep purple-tinted mahogany palette to fit a high-fantasy anime aesthetic with gold accents.

Settling on warm walnut tones for the shelves and a midnight blue frame trim, with the back panel getting an indigo gradient sprinkled with stars. I'm working out how to generate the star pattern using a cell-noise function evaluated on a flattened 2D plane, since the paint function operates on 3D vectors but the back panel only varies in x and y.

Confirming mix() works fine with color string arguments, so I can blend hex colors directly in the paint callback. I'm tweaking the star dot radius a bit larger since the texel size is coarser than my initial estimate, and noting the back panel stars will mostly peek through gaps between books. Now I'm writing a hash function that mixes integer coordinates with multiplication and XOR shifts to produce pseudo-random noise values.

Setting up the imports from the SDK and starting to build the bookshelf structure with a root joint, then defining small helper functions to simplify creating boxes and other parts attached to that root.

I'll keep spheres smooth rather than low-poly for that glass-like look, and orient cylinders along the x-axis using a direction vector. Now I'm starting to lay out the cabinet dimensions as constants.

Adding gold rings and capitals to the columns at various heights, and considering a simple gold trim strip along each board's front edge instead of more elaborate hanging ornaments to keep the detailing manageable.

I'm picking out a palette of twelve saturated anime-style colors for the book covers—crimson, royal blue, emerald, violet, teal, amber, rose, indigo, burgundy, forest, ivory, and midnight—to vary the bookshelf visually while averaging around 5.5 parts per book by only giving bands and plates to about half of them.
